newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Race for EMU raises doubts over budgetary rigour.
newsitem.headline: Race for EMU raises doubts over budgetary rigour.

text.p: The frantic race among European Union governments to qualify for a common currency in 1999 has led a growing number to play a budgetary numbers game that puts short-term expediency above all else.

Analysts and EU monetary officials say the governments of France, Belgium, Italy and Spain have announced budgets for 1997 which contain a questionable dose of creative accounting and one-off items designed to qualify for monetary union.

The intense focus on 1997, the year in which aspiring governments must bring their deficits near three percent of Gross Domestic Product in order to join monetary union, may mask what is ultimately important -- sustainable economic and budgetary convergence.
"What we have to look at is durable convergence," said one monetary official, dismayed at the obsession over 1997 budget figures.
"When you read the (Maastricht) treaty, the durability issue is very much stressed," he added.

Among the most brazen in their interpretation of EU accounting law is France, which plans to add a whopping 37.5 billion francs ($7.4 billion) to its budget next year through the process of privatising France Telecom.

The European Commission, the EU executive, has yet to decide whether France's creative use of privatisation funds is legitimate, but recent remarks from Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy suggest they are leaning in that direction.

Italy, meanwhile, has included a special one-off "Euro tax" to help it bring its finances under control in 1997, and Spain, desperate to be among the first wave of single currency members, has been criticised for overly optimistic growth projections and a freeze on public sector wages.
"In reality, this group of creative accounting measures do nothing but delay the deficit to future years," said Jose Borrell, budget spokesman for Spain's Socialist Workers' Party on Sunday.
Indeed, economists say the glowing endorsement European financial markets have given the latest spate of budget news from Rome and Madrid is probably overdone.

"The markets maybe shouldn't take the raw numbers too seriously," warns Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in London, who agreed that a fast and loose approach with budgets raises "an awful lot of questions about durable convergence."
The desire to fudge numbers extends further north as well, with Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene set on Tuesday to unveil a 1997 budget which has come under attack from private economists.
Elements of the budget have already emerged, including the sum of 80 billion Belgian francs ($2.55 billion) to cover a package of increases in indirect taxes and spending cuts.

Economists said it contained a number of one-off measures, such as the sale of gold coins, taken in part to avoid any drastic cuts in heavy spending areas such as social security, which would be hugely unpopular.
"Most European countries are trying to cure a hangover by having another drink," said economist Christer Lindholm at J.P. Morgan in Brussels.

The failure of many EU governments to engage in meaningful structural budget reform is perhaps to be expected given the political risks involved, but some say the criticism of countries like Italy and Spain may be a bit harsh.
Taken in context, both countries have come a long way from the free-wheeling days of hefty spending increases financed by an ever-rising stream of debt.
"I think in both cases (Spain and Italy), these are major changes and a clear break with the past," said an EU monetary official.
